🥳 Happy Friday! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,378 words ... 5 mins. Thanks to Noah Bressner for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

🗳️ Vibe check ... Lead story on The Wall Street Journal's site when I woke up: "Weeks Before the Midterms, Almost Everything Is Getting More Expensive ... The price of eating out, filling a gas tank and buying a house keeps rising, while higher interest rates add to borrowing costs." Gift link.
 
 
1 big thing: "Most contentious interview"
 
Axios' Alex Thompson interviews Hasan Piker in his L.A. home on Wednesday. Photo: Michael Rossetti for Axios

In the new episode of "The Axios Show," out this morning, left-wing streamer Hasan Piker said he "absolutely" wants to campaign for New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez if she runs for president in 2028 and said he has talked with AOC and her team.

  • Why it matters: Piker, who has millions of followers online, has been a high-profile campaign surrogate this year for a new generation of left-wing candidates, and wants to do the same in 2028.

In an hourlong interview with Axios' Alex Thompson that Piker later described as his "most contentious" ever, the Twitch star defended his stances that some Democrats are recoiling from:

China: Piker traveled to China last year and has said that the country is the closest government model he would like to see adopted in the U.S.

  • He also thinks that "trajectory-wise, I worry that a Chinese child might have better conditions in the next decade or next two decades than an American one. And I think that should worry every American citizen."

Asked about his past praise of Mao Zedong, Piker said: "He's a great man of history. Of course, there were a lot of excesses."

  • When asked to clarify what he meant by "excesses," Piker said: "Deaths borne out of mismanagement and famine."
Hasan Piker and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez speak at Zohran Mamdani's election night rally in Brooklyn last November. Photo: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Political violence: Axios asked Piker about several of his past statements about killing or harming political opponents, and he said they amounted to "three or four choice quotes."

  • He said he consistently says that the "appropriate way to deal with political problems, even violent ones, is to advocate, organize, and create a response that is borne out of labor militancy, work stoppages and the like, to apply political pressure that way."
  • Talking with a friend on his stream, Piker once said of landlords who don't rent their properties: "Kill those motherf*ckers and murder those motherf*ckers in the streets. Let the streets soak in their f*cking red capitalist blood, dude."
  • He told Axios that "we were messing around. It wasn't a serious call to violence."

Piker — a frequent and aggressive critic of Israel's government — said he believes "Zionism is fascism" and that it was equivalent to neo-Nazism.

  • Asked about the potential danger of his rhetoric, Piker said: "I'm not worried that [my followers are] going to be violent against Zionists. No, I'm not."

2. 🐊 Fear and loathing in Trump's backyard
 

Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios
 

Axios' Marc Caputo, a Miami Herald alumnus, writes from his Miami home:

Staring into the camera, Rep. Maria Salazar cut a new campaign ad that told President Trump what so many of her fellow Hispanic Republicans in Miami are saying: The immigration crackdown has gone too far.

  • Why it matters: The anger at Trump over heavy-handed immigration enforcement is palpable in Miami-Dade County, and there's mounting political worry among Republicans across the state that it could cost the GOP in the midterm elections.

🔎 Zoom in: A bellwether, Miami-Dade is Florida's most populous county, which Trump flipped to the Republican column in 2020 and 2024 thanks to strong Latino support, especially among Cuban Americans.

  • "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in her ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
  • Trump carried her district by 15 points two years ago. Today, she's tied in polls with newscaster Eliot Rodriguez, a fellow Cuban American, who said her new ad was a sign of desperation.

A Trump adviser told Axios: "I'm getting the Trumpiest Cubans sending me videos from Miami of guys getting busted at places like the gas station, for no apparent reason."

  • A GOP pollster from Miami said: "Support is just evaporating. The economy sucks and ICE is just out of control. People feel they didn't sign up for this."

3. 🦾 Claude helping build its next version
 
Chart: Anthropic

Claude is helping Anthropic develop the next, more intelligent version of itself, the AI lab announced:

  • "Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work," Anthropic said. "Claude 'leads' 26% of Anthropic's AI R&D work."

Why it matters: The announcement was unclear about how close the company believes it is to achieving recursive self-improvement (RSI, when AI builds itself). But the pace at which Claude is increasingly contributing to research and development is escalating, AP notes:

  • The portion of work Claude "leads," or does in large part while remaining under human supervision, was zero in February. Six months later, in August, it was 26%.

4. 🤷 Stumping Wall Street
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep. Chart: Axios/Emily Peck

JPMorgan analysts offered an unusually blunt assessment of the oil market: They have no idea what happens next.

  • "For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don't have a baseline view. We simply don't know how to model the endgame."

Why it matters: Market watchers have come to grips with the likelihood that the status of the Strait of Hormuz — and the number of barrels getting through — will be messy for months to come, Axios' Ben Geman writes.

  • Go deeper with Axios Future of Energy.
 
 
5. 🤖 Inside the scramble for trusted AI cops
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

A host of industry players, policy wonks and businesses are grappling with the question of how to regulate AI in a trustworthy manner.

  • Inside the White House, it's mostly business as usual, Axios' Maria Curi reports.

Why it matters: The industry's mad dash stems from an ad hoc regulatory apparatus. But swift action from Washington is unlikely.

🎨 The big picture: An ecosystem of safety and benchmarking groups already exists. But some White House officials and AI execs see them as too closely tied to top AI companies.

  • Other options include businesses and startups that already do evaluations.

6. 🇻🇪 Scoop: Trump plans Venezuela sit-down
 
President Trump hosted a dinner for 100+ hunters and fishermen in the Rose Garden last night. Photo: Alex Brandon/AP

President Trump is planning a first-ever meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, as early as Tuesday, sources familiar with the discussions tell Axios' Marc Caputo.

  • Why it matters: The potential meeting showcases the close relations between the nations under Trump. But it's also fraught with political risks that stretch from Miami to Caracas.

👀 Behind the scenes: Trump is already planning to meet with Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York next week to discuss the Iran war, and those who know his thinking say he wants to make time for a sideline sit-down with Rodríguez, sources said.

  • A Trump adviser told Axios: "Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that. Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time."
  • A senior administration official cautioned: "Nothing is finalized. This is up to the president."

7. 🗞️ NYT @ 175
 
Photo: Sara Fischer/Axios

The first issue of The New York Times was published 175 years ago today, on Sept. 18, 1851.

  • Above: At a birthday party in Manhattan last night, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Mark Thompson — CEO of CNN Worldwide and former CEO of The New York Times Company — watch Pulitzer-winning Times reporters Megan Twohey and Jodi Kantor salute Ashley Judd for being the first actress to speak out against Harvey Weinstein.
Images: The New York Times

Then and now ... New York Times front pages, 175 years apart.

8. 🍌 1 fun thing: Parties go bananas
 
Attendees at the "eat an apple with me" event in D.C. last month. Photo: Tierney L. Cross for The Washington Post via Getty Images

Young people are showing up by the hundreds for parties built around absurdly niche premises, Axios D.C.'s Mimi Montgomery writes.

  • There's a party happening this weekend in D.C. that's BYOB — Bring Your Own Banana.
  • A recent "eat an apple with me" party drew hundreds out to Washington's Meridian Hill Park.
  • Other greatest hits include a "Smoke a Cigarette With Me" party that brought 1,500 people together to rip cigs in New York's Washington Square Park. Hundreds gathered to watch a dude in Philly eat a rotisserie chicken.

Why it matters: The premise is almost beside the point. It's a low-stakes excuse to hang out in real life at a time when loneliness is widespread and young people are drinking less.
